title: Satellites That Watch the Weather
summary: How weather satellites orbit Earth, what their sensors measure, and how forecasters use their information to predict the weather and warn people.
poll: Weather satellites are the most important tool for keeping people safe from storms.

versions.title: Eyes in the Sky
versions.text:
Look up. You can not see it. A machine is up in space. It looks down at you. It is a satellite. It helps us know the sky.

It goes round and round our planet. This path is its orbit. The sun gives it power. It has big flat wings. They catch the sun.

The first one went up in 1960. It sent back a shot of clouds. No one had seen clouds like that from space.

There are two kinds. One kind is very, very high. It keeps up with Earth as Earth spins. So it looks at the same spot all the time. It sends new shots in a few minutes.

The other kind is low. It goes from pole to pole. The Earth spins below it. So it sees the whole planet, strip by strip.

Some shots are like a photo. They show the clouds by day. Some show heat. They work at night, too. A cold cloud top is a sign of a tall storm cloud.

How does this help? We can see a storm on its way. We can see dust blow. Then we can forecast the rain and wind. We can warn folks.

versions.title: Satellites That Watch the Weather
versions.text:
Look up at the sky. You cannot see them, but high above you, machines are watching Earth. They are weather satellites, and they watch the weather day and night.

A satellite travels around our planet again and again along a path called an orbit. Why doesn't it fall? It moves sideways very fast. Gravity pulls it toward Earth, but its speed carries it around the curve of the planet. It gets its power from the sun through large solar panels.

The first weather satellite, called TIROS-1, was launched in 1960. It sent back the first TV picture of clouds taken from space.

There are two main kinds of weather satellites. One kind orbits about 36,000 kilometers above the equator. It moves at the same speed as Earth spins, so it stays above the same region. It can send new pictures every few minutes.

The other kind orbits much lower, about 800 kilometers up. It passes over the North and South Poles. As Earth turns beneath it, it scans the whole planet, one strip at a time.

Each satellite carries sensors. Some sensors take pictures like a camera, but they only work in daylight. Infrared sensors measure heat, so they work at night as well. Very cold cloud tops show tall storm clouds.

The satellites send what they collect to stations on the ground by radio. Forecasters use it to track storms, cyclones, and dust. Computers mix it with other measurements to forecast the weather. Then people can be warned in time.

It receives its electrical power from the sun through large solar panels.

Because they travel at the same speed as Earth rotates, they remain above the same region and can deliver new images every few minutes, which makes them ideal for watching storms develop.

Powerful computers combine it with other measurements to forecast the weather, which allows communities to be warned in time.

versions.title: Satellites That Watch the Weather
versions.text:
Although you cannot see them with the naked eye when gazing upward, machines are nevertheless continuously observing the Earth from far above the surface. These are weather satellites, and they monitor the atmosphere ceaselessly, day and night alike, sending an uninterrupted stream of valuable information down to scientists stationed on the ground below.

A satellite travels around our planet repeatedly along a fixed path called an orbit, staying aloft not through any defiance of gravity but because it moves sideways at tremendous speed, and although gravity continuously pulls it toward Earth, its considerable sideways motion carries it around the curvature of the planet in a steady, self-sustaining balance. Such a satellite gets its needed electrical power from the sun itself, through extensive solar panels mounted on its exterior.

The very first weather satellite, called TIROS-1, was launched by the United States in 1960. Although its photographs look quite blurry by today's standards, it still sent the first television image of clouds ever captured from space, and scientists immediately saw the immense value such a high vantage point could offer. Before satellites existed at all, a dangerous storm forming far out at sea could approach a coastline with very little warning, since ships and weather stations were often absent from the area to observe its approach.

Two main kinds of weather satellite exist today. Geostationary satellites orbit at roughly 36,000 kilometers directly above the equator, and because they travel at exactly the same speed at which the Earth itself turns, they stay fixed above the same region, delivering fresh images every few minutes, a capability that makes them ideally suited for watching storms as they actively develop.

Polar-orbiting satellites, by contrast, travel much lower, roughly 800 kilometers above the surface, passing over the North and South Poles about fourteen times a day. As the Earth turns steadily beneath them, these satellites scan the entire planet one narrow strip at a time, giving a closer and more detailed view than their geostationary counterparts.

Each satellite also carries a set of specialized sensors. Certain instruments capture visible images like an ordinary camera, though these work only during daylight hours, whereas infrared sensors measure heat directly and so keep working through the night as well, with extremely cold cloud tops reliably revealing towering, potentially dangerous storm clouds. Additional sensors measure atmospheric water vapor, the largely invisible moisture spread through the air, which helps forecasters predict where clouds and rain are likely to form.

Once the satellites send their gathered measurements to ground stations by radio, meteorologists then use this information to track developing storms, tropical cyclones forming over the Arabian Sea, and dust sweeping across the desert, while powerful computer systems combine it with other data to generate forecasts that let whole communities be warned well in advance.

versions.title: Satellites That Watch the Weather
versions.text:
Although you cannot discern them with the unaided eye when gazing skyward, sophisticated machines are nevertheless continuously observing the Earth from far above its surface. These are weather satellites, and they monitor the planet's atmosphere ceaselessly, throughout both day and night alike, transmitting an uninterrupted stream of valuable observational data down to scientists stationed on the ground below.

A satellite traverses our planet repeatedly along a fixed trajectory termed an orbit, remaining aloft not through any defiance of fundamental physical law but because it travels laterally at tremendous orbital velocity; although gravity continuously exerts its pull toward Earth, the satellite's considerable sideways momentum simultaneously carries it around the curvature of the planet in a perpetual, self-sustaining gravitational balance. Such a satellite derives its necessary electrical power from the sun itself, by means of extensive solar panels mounted upon its exterior surfaces.

The very first weather satellite, designated TIROS-1, was launched into orbit by the United States in 1960. Although its photographic output appears decidedly blurry by contemporary technological standards, it nevertheless transmitted the first television image of clouds ever successfully captured from the vantage point of outer space, and scientists immediately recognized the immense practical value such an elevated perspective could offer meteorology as a discipline. Before satellites existed at all, a dangerous storm developing far out at sea could approach a populated coastline with remarkably little advance warning, since ships and weather stations were frequently absent from the immediate vicinity to observe its gradual approach.

Two principal categories of weather satellite exist in operational use today. Geostationary satellites orbit at an altitude of approximately 36,000 kilometers directly above the equator, and because they travel at precisely the identical angular speed at which the Earth itself rotates, they remain perpetually positioned above the same fixed geographic region, continuously delivering updated images every few minutes, a capability that renders them ideally suited for observing storms as they actively develop, intensify, and evolve over time.

Polar-orbiting satellites, by contrast, travel at a considerably lower orbital altitude, approximately 800 kilometers above the surface, passing over the North and South Poles roughly fourteen separate times within a single day. As the Earth rotates steadily beneath them in the interim, these satellites systematically scan the entire planet one narrow strip at a time, thereby providing a closer and substantially more granularly detailed perspective than their geostationary counterparts can typically achieve.

Each satellite additionally carries an extensive array of specialized sensors. Certain instruments capture visible images in the manner of a conventional camera, though these function exclusively during daylight hours, whereas infrared sensors measure emitted heat directly and therefore continue operating effectively throughout the night as well, with extremely cold cloud tops reliably revealing the presence of towering, potentially hazardous storm clouds below. Additional sensors measure atmospheric water vapor, the largely invisible moisture dispersed throughout the atmosphere, which assists forecasters considerably in anticipating precisely where clouds and subsequent precipitation are likely to develop.

Once the satellites transmit their accumulated measurements to ground stations by radio signal, meteorologists subsequently employ this continuous stream of information to monitor developing storms, tropical cyclones forming over the Arabian Sea, and dust sweeping across the desert interior, while powerful computer systems simultaneously integrate it with other observational data sources to generate increasingly accurate forecasts that allow entire communities to be warned well in advance of approaching hazards.

MID.prompt: Compare the two main kinds of weather satellites. Explain how each one helps forecasters, using details from the article.
checklist: I described both kinds of satellites.
I explained one way each kind helps forecasters.
I used details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: There are two main kinds of weather satellites. One kind orbits about 36,000 kilometers above the equator and moves at the same speed as Earth spins, so it stays over the same region and sends new pictures every few minutes. The other kind orbits much lower, about 800 kilometers up, and passes over the poles, scanning the whole planet one strip at a time as Earth turns beneath it. The first kind helps forecasters watch a storm develop quickly, while the second kind helps them see the entire globe using infrared sensors.

keyWords.example: A geostationary satellite always appears in the same place in the sky.

keyWords.definition: describing invisible light given off by warm objects, which special tools can detect as heat
keyWords.example: Firefighters use infrared cameras to find people in smoke-filled rooms.

keyWords.definition: the imaginary circle around Earth halfway between the North and South Poles
keyWords.example: Day and night are almost equal in length all year near the equator.

keyWords.definition: a device that detects and measures something such as light, heat, or moisture
keyWords.example: A sensor in the greenhouse turns on the sprinklers when the soil is dry.

keyWords.definition: the layer of gases surrounding Earth
keyWords.example: Earth's atmosphere protects us from much of the sun's harmful light.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how weather satellites have changed the way people prepare for dangerous weather. Support your answer with evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how satellites help people prepare.
I used at least two specific pieces of evidence.
I organized my ideas clearly with an introduction and conclusion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Weather satellites have changed the way people prepare for dangerous weather by giving forecasters a constant view of the entire planet. For instance, geostationary satellites stay above the same region near the equator and send new pictures every few minutes, allowing forecasters to track a storm as it forms. In addition, infrared sensors can measure heat and detect tall storm clouds even at night, which older methods could not do. Because of this technology, computers can combine the data to create forecasts that warn people of cyclones and dust storms before they strike. In conclusion, satellites have given people far more warning time than ever before.
